text: When pigs stop eating with morning fever above 40°C and no other obvious signs yet (other symptoms often appear 2–3 days later as the underlying disease develops), common causes include: septicemia (bacteria spreading through the bloodstream, causing acute severe weakness, high fever, and loss of appetite); a retained dead piglet or retained afterbirth after farrowing (fever develops a few days postpartum, with discharge appearing later if septicemia hasn't already set in); other bacterial septicemias (e.g. Erysipelas); cystitis progressing to kidney infection (pyelonephritis) and then septicemia; and atypical CSF (persistent high fever unresponsive to antibiotics should always bring CSF to mind — a follow-up visit and necropsy a few days later can confirm typical CSF lesions). Treatment: inject a broad-spectrum antibiotic as soon as possible (Enrofloxacin or Tetracycline, double dose), and Paracetamol to lower fever (it is gentler on the stomach wall than some alternatives).
